Upon the revocation of the edict of Nantes, when the persecution commenced against; the Protestants, SchombersJ, who was of that persuasion, requested leave to retire into his own country. This request was refused'; but he was permitted to take refuge in Portugal, where he had reason to expect he would be kindly re* ceived on account of past services. But the religious zeal of the Portugucfe, though it did not prevent them from accepting afiillance from a heretic when their {kingdom was threatened with subversion, could not permit them to give him (helter when he came for protection. The inquisition interfered, and obliged the king; to send him away. He then went to Holland by the ■way of England. Having accepted an invitation from the elector of Brandenburg, he was invested with the government of Ducal Prussia, and appointed commander in chief of the eledlor's forces. When the prince of Orange failed to England to take possession of the crown w^hich his father-in law James H. had abdicated, ♦Schomberg obtained permission from the elector of Brandenburg to accompany him. He is supposed to have been the author of an ingenious stratagem which the prince employed after his arrival in London to discover the sentiments of tile people refpedling the revolution. The stratagem was, to spread an alarm over the country that the Irish were approaching with fire and sword. When the prince was eflabliflied on the throne of England, Schomberg was appointed commander in chief of the forces and master of the ordnance. In April J 689 he was made knight of the garter, and naturalized by aft of Parliament ; and in May foUowmjr was created a baron, earl, marquis, and duke of the kingdom of England, by the name and title of baron Tcys, earl of Brentford, marquis of Harwich, and duke of Schomberg. The Ploufe of Commons voted to him L. 100,000 as a rew-ard for his fersices. Of this he only received a small part ; but aixer his death a pension of L. 5000 a-year was bestowed upon his fon.

In August 1689 he was sent to Ireland to reduce that kirf;dom to obedience. When he arrived, he found himself at the head of an army consisting only of 1 2,000 foot and looo horse, while king James commanded an army three times more numerous. Schomberg thought it dangerous to engage with so superior a force, and being disappointed in his promised fupphes from England, judged it prudent to remain on the defensive. He therefore ported himself at Dundalk, about five or six miles cliftance from James, who wa* encamped at Ardee. For six weeks he remained in this position, without attempting to give battle, while from the wetness of the season he loll nearly the half of his army. Schomberg was much blamed for not coming to ail;ion ; but some excellent judges admired his conduct as a display of great military talents, iriad he risked an engagement, and tecii defeated, Ireland would have been loft. At the famous battle of the Boyne, fought on the lit July 1690, which decided ihti fate of James, Schomberg passed the river at the head of his cavalry, defeated eight squadrons of the enemy, and broke the Irifli infantry. W^hen the French Protestants loft their commander, Schomberg went to rally and lead them on to charge. While thus engaged, a party of king James's guards, which had been separated from the reft, passed SchomS C H

berg, in attempting to rejoin their own army. They attacked him with great fuiy, and gave him two wounds in the head. As the wourKls were not dangerous, he might soon have recovered from them ; but the French Protestants, perhaps thinking their general was killed, immediately fired upon the guards, and Shot him dead on the Ipot. He was buried in St Patrick's cathedral.

Bishop Burnet fays, Schomberg was " a calm man, of great application and conduct, and thought much better than he spoke ; of true judgment, of exact probity, and of a humble and obliging temper."

1 he Hebrews were always very diligent to teach and study the laws that they had received from Moses. The father of the family studied and taught them in his own family. They pretend, that even before the deluge there were fchoulsfor knowledge and piety, of which the patriarchs had the direction. — U hey place Adam at their head, then Enoch, and laftly Noah. Melchisedec, as they say, kept a school in the city of Kajrath sepher, otherwise Hebron, in Palestine. Abraham, who had been instruct ted by Heber, taught in ^Chaldoea and in Egypt. From him the Egyptians learned astronomy a"nd arithmetic. Jacob succeeded Abraham in the of ice of teaching. I'he scripture says, he was '* a plain man dwelling in tents;" which, according to the Ghaldee paraphrast, is, " that he was a perfect man, and a minister of the house of doctrine."

All this, indeed, must be very precarious and uncertain. It cannot be doubted but that Moses, Aaron, and the elders of Israel, inftruded the people in the wilderness, and that many good Israelites wc'-e very industrious to instruct their families in the fear of God. But ill this does not prove to us that there were any such schools as we are now inquiring after. Under JoIhua we fee a kind of academy of the prophets, wiiere the children of the prophets, that is, their difcipks, lived ill the exercise of a retired and austere life, in study, in the meditation and reading of the law of God. 'i here were schools of the prophets at Naioth in Ramah; 1 Sam. xix, 12, 20, &c. See the article Prophet.

Sunday'ScHoois are another species of charity-schools lately instituted, and now pretty common in Great Bri. tain. The institution is evidently of the first importance ; and if properly encouraged must have a yciy favourable eff del on the morals of the people, as it tends not only to preserve the children of the poor from spending Sunday in idleness, and of consequence in dissipation and vice, but enables them to lay in for the conduct and comfort of their future life a stock of useful knowledge and virtuous principles, which, if neglected in early life, will seldom be fought for or obtained amidst the ii urry of businese and the cai-es and temptations of the world.

The excelknt founder of Sunday-schools wa« Mr Raikes, a gentleman of Gloucefterftiire, who^ together with Mr Stock, a clergyman in the same county, and who, we believe, was equally inftruniental in the business with Mr Raikes, site wed the example, and con vin- «ed many of the utility of the plan. Its structure is made up of fine cylindric columns, like needles collected into bundles or trefles, lying one on another in different directions, whilst each individual column is made up of fine plates or laminje, like the gems. It is fusible per se into a white transparent glass, and melts imperfectly with borax when calcined, as it does with microcosmic fait and mineral alkali, into a small vitreous globe,, with little spots of a white enamel colour. The ftriK^burse of the semitransparent fehei-ls, and some of the transparent that are not so perfectly dia» phanous as to conceal their texture, is obscurely sparry; . but that of the opaque is either filamentous, like af-- bestes, or hard and brittle like threade of glase, or it is composed of scales. The ruby-cok>ured schorl - mentioned af cove was found by Mr Herman at Sarapoulfky, a village in the government of Perm, ten versts from Mourfinfky Slabode, in Siberia. The Siberian infpe<stor, Mr Laxman, has lately discovered in - the mountain Alpeftria, on the river Sbudenka near the lake Baikal, the folio wing new schorls. SCHULTENS (Albert), prose stor of Hebrew and of the eastern languages at Leyden, and one of the most learned men of the i8th century, was born at Groningen, where he studied till the year 17^6, and from thence continued his studies at Leyden and Utrecht. Schultens at length applied himself to the study of Arabic books, both printed and in manuscript ; in which he made great progress. A short time after he became minister of Walfenar, and two years after professor of the eastern tongues at Franeker. At length he was invited to Leyden, where he taught Hebrew and the eastern languages with extraordinary reputation till his death, which happened in 1750. He wrote many learned works ; the principal of which are, i. A Commentary on Job, 2 vols 4to. 2. A Commentary on the Proverbs. 3. Vetus Cff regta via Hebrai%and't. 4. Animailvfr (tones philologica critic et ad varia lora Veteris Teil ment. 6. An excellent Hetrew grammar, &c. Schultens discovered in all his works found criticism and much learning. He maintain- €d against Gouffet and Driest en, that in order to have a perfect knowledge of Hebrew, it is neceflkry to join with it, not only the Chaldee and Syriac, but more particularly the Arabic.

SCHURMAN (Anna-Maria), a most extraordinary German lady. Her natural genius discovered itself at §x years of age, when ftie cut all forts of figures in

paper with her scissors without a pattern. At eight, S^h fhe learned, in a few days, to draw flowers in a very agreeable manner. At ten, (he took but three hours ^eo,' to learn embroidery. ■ Afterwards fhe was taught music, vocal and instrumental ; painting, sculpture, and engraving ; in all of which fhe succeeded admirably. She excelled in miniature-painting, and in cutting portraits upon glass with a diamond. Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, were so familiar to her, that the most learned men were astonished at it. She spoke French, Italian, and English, fluently. Her handwriting, in almost all languages, was so inimitable, that the curious preserved specimens of it in their cabinets. But all this extent of learning and uncommon penetration could not protest her from falling into the errors of Labadie, the famous French enthusiast, who had been banished France for his extravagant tenets and conduA. To this man (he entirely attached herself, and accompanied him wherever he went ; and even attended him in his last illness at Altena in Holstein. Her works, consisting oi De vile humane term 'tno, and D'tjfertatio de ingenii muUebrts ad doSrinam et meliores Iter as apt'itudine^ and her Letters to her learned correspondents, were printed at Leyden in 1648 ; but enlarged in the edition of Utrecht, 1662, In i2mo, under the following title : A. M. Schurman Opuscula Heb roof Graca^ Lotina, Gallica, Prosaica, et Mettica. She pu wished hkewlfe at Altena, in Latin, A Defence of her attachment to Labadie, while fhe was with him in 1673 ; not worth reading. She was born at Cologne in 1607, but resided chiefly in Holland, and died in Fricfland in 1678.

SCHWARTS (Christopher), an eminent history. painter, born at Ingolftadt in 1550, who was distinguished by the appellation of the German Raphael. He learned the first principles of the art in his own country, but finished his studies at Venice ; when he not only made the works of Titian his models, but had the advantage of receiving some personal instruct lens from that illustrious master. His performances were soon in the highest esteem, as his manner of painting was very different from what the Germans had been accustomed to before that time : he was, therefore, invited by the elector of Bavaria to his court, and appointed his principal painter. He died in 1594; and his most capital works, as well in fresco as in oil, are in the palace at Munich, and in the churches and convents.

science.c:
SCIENCE, In philosophy, denotes any doctrine deduced from self-evident principles.

Sciences may be properly divided as follows, i. The knowledge of things, their constitutions,. properties, and operations : this, in a little more enlarged sense of the w«rd, may be called ?>tar<i(.w^ or natural philosophy i the end of which is speculative truth. See Philosophy and Physics. — 2. The flclli of rightly ap. plying these powers, 'rfxurixH j The most considerable under this head is ethics, which Is the seeking out those rides and measures of human actions that lead to happiness, and the means to practise them (see Morai. Philosophy) ; and the next is mechanics, or the application of the powers of natural agents to the uf^s of life (see Mechakiics). — 3. This dod trine of signs, (r«Mti«Tixw } the most usual of which being words, it ife aptly enough termed logic. See Logic.

This, says Mr Locke, seems to be the most general, as well as natural, division of the objects of our understanding. For a man can employ his thoughts about nothing but either the contemplation of things themselves for the discovery of truth ; or about the things in his own power, which are his adlions, for the attainment ef his own ends ; or the signs the mind makes use of both in the one and the other, and the right ordering of them for its clearer information. AH which three, nnx. things as they are in themselves know able, aliens as they depend on us in order to happiness, and the right use of signs in order to knowledge, being toto case different, they seem to be the three great provinces of the intellectual world, wholly separate and distinct one from another.

These islands were first calfed Cafjitendes:, or the Tin IJIes, from their being rich in that metal, 'i'he common opinion is, tliat this is a Greek appellation ; \K hich in the mast obvious fen-se is true : But as the Phccnicians were familiar with the metal, and with the country that produced it, before the Gieeks knew any thing of either, it is very likely they introduced the names of both from their own language. The riches of these islands were tin and lead, ^.vhich, with the skins of their cattle, they exclianged Avith foreign merchants, that is, the Plioenicians from Cadiz, for e?.rthen-ware, fait, and utensils made of strass. An author of as great or greater antiquity, ii'ems to include a part at least of Cornwall amonoft t^ese islands ; or rather hefuggefts, that they were not persea islands except at full sea, but that at ebbrhe inhabitants painted from one to another upon the fands, and that they evert transported their tin in lai-ge ftjuare blocks upon carriages from one island to another. -He farther takes notice, that fir*» •s inJiabited about Befcrium (the Sarid'^s End) vvere in their conversation ■^ith strangers remarkably civil and coin-tt-,^uS. Qther ancient writers style these islands He/pend s, from ■^air western situation, and Oeflrymnidesy asserting that ■lie laud was extremely fertile, as well as f*ll of mines ; SMFid that the people, though very brave, were entirely addicted to commerce, and boldly passed the seas^ in: ^cir leather boats.

The Romans were exceedingly desirous of having a* Siare in this commerce, which the Phceniciaa* as care-- filly 1-abomed to prevent, by concealing their navigation to these iflaads as much as it was in their power. At length, however, the Romans prevailed ; and Publius ifcrafiiw coif ting tliidier, ^fi9s fa \*c-ll: pleased withthe

Induilry and maimers of txie people, tliat he taught them various improvements, as well in working their mines, which till that time wtre but Hi allow, as in carrying their own merchandise to different markets. When the legions were withdrawn, and Britain with its dependencies left inthe power of the natives, there is no reason to question that these islands fiiared th^ same lot v/iththe rest. As to the appellation -vvhicli from this period prevailed, the ordinary way of writing it is Scilly ; in records we commonly lind it spelt Si/ly, Sllley, or Sulley ; but we are told the old Britifli appellation' was Sulleh, or Sylleh, which signifies. rocks consecrated to the sun. We have not the least notice of any thing that regards them from the fifth to the tenth century. It is, however, with mucli. appearance of truth conjectured, that some time withiii, this space they were in a great measure destroyed by an earthquake, attended with a sink sig of the earth, by which molt of their lowlands, and of course the greateil part of their improvements, were covered' by the se?., and those rich m.ines of tin \7hich had rendered them so famous swa}U)wed up in the deep.. They have a tradition inCornwall, that a very often>- five tia6t of country called the L'mncfi, in the old' Cornifli Lfthoufoiv, supposed to lie between that country and Scilly, was loft in that manner ; and there are many concurrent circumstances which render this probably^. Thi-s sufficiently proves the fast, that by such an earthquake they wfei'tdeilroyed ; and that it happened at som.e period of time with sit those limits that have been' assigned, appears frfr>m our hearing nothing more of their tin trade, and from? our having no notice of it at all in any of our ancient chronicles, which, if it had fallen out later, from thtir known attention to extraordinary events, must certainly have happe-ied.

The Scllly, or Sllley islands, lie due weft front the Lizard about 17 kagues ; weft and by soil th from the old Land's End, next Mount's Bay, at the distance of 10 leagues ; and from the western Land's End, they lie wert-iouth-west, at the distance of something moie than nine leagues. The remairts of the abbey are yet visible, the situation well chosen, with a fine bason of fret li water before it, half a mile long and a furlong wide, with an ever-gie en bank high enough to keep out the sea, and serving at once to preserve the pond, and shelter the abbey. This island is particularly noted for producing plenty of the finest samphire, and the only tin works that are now visible are found here> There are upon it at present about 40 families, who are very industrious, and spin more wool than in St Mary's. A mile to the east of Trefcaw, and about two miles from the most northern part of St Mary's, lies the isle of St Martin's, not much inferior in size to that of Trefcaw. It very plainly appears to have been formerly e?extremely well cultivated; notwithstanding which it was entirely deserted, till within somewhat less than a century ago, that Mr Thomas Ekiwes, a confiderable merchant, engaged some people to fettle there. Fle likewise caused to be erected a hollow tower twenty feet in height, with a spire of as many feet more ; which being neatly covered with lime, ferves Is a daymai-kfor dlrefting fi lips crofTmgthe channel or comln;'- into Scllly. St Martin's produces some corn, afford'a the best past tire in these islands, nourishes a great number of flieep, and has upon it 1 7 families, who pretend to have the secret of burning the best kelp, and are ex- ^extremely attached to their own island. As a proof of this, it Is observable, that though some of the Inhabitants rent lands in St Mary's, yet they continue to reside here, going thither only occasionally.

St Jgnes, which is also called the Llght-houst: Island, lies near three miles south-Vveft of St Marj-'s ; and is, tho sigh a very little, a very well cultivated island, fruitful ^ in corn and grass. ■ The only inconvenience to which the people who live in it are subjest, is the want of good water, as th«ir capital advantage consists in havmg several good coves or final ports, where boats may he with safety ; which, however, are not much used. The light ho use is the principal ornament and great support of the island, which stands on the most elevated ground, built with stone from the foundation to the saul horn, which is fiity-one feet high, the gallery four, the fafli-lights eleven feet and a half high, three feet two Inches wide, and sixteen in number. Upon the whole, it is noble and commodious structure'; and being plastered white, is a useful dayjBfiark to all ships coming from the southward. The keeper of this light-house has a salary from the Trinityhoufe at Deptford of 40 1. a-yeast, with a dwelling, house and ground for a garden. His assistant has 20 1. a-year. • It is fupphed with coals by an annual (hip ; and the carriage of these coals from the sea-side to the li;^ht-house is looked on as a considerable benefit to the poor inhabitants. They have a neat little church, built by the Godolphin family. There are at present 50 households in the island, which yield the propiietor 40L a-year.

Brehar, or, as pronounced, Bryer island, lies northwest of St Mary's, and to the weft of Trefcaw, to ■which, when the sea 13 very low, they sometimes pass over the fand. It is very mountainous, abounds with sea and land fowls, excellent samphire, and a great variety of medical herbs. There are at present thirteen fa mines, who have a pretty church, and pay 30 1. a-year to the proprietor.

South from hence, and weft from Trefcaw, stands the island of Samson, in which there is not above one family, who subsist chiefly by the making of kelp. To the westward of these there lie four ' islands, which contain in the whole 360 acres of meadow and arable land. The eajiern tile sy so denominated from their position in respect to St Mary's, contain 123 acres; and there are also seven other rocky and scattered islands, that have each a little land "of some use ; and besides these, innumerable rocks on every side, among which we must reckon Sci/ly, now nothing more than a large, ill-shaped, craggy, inaccessible island, lying the farthest north-weft of any of them, and consequently the nearest to the continent.

Th* air of these islands is equally mild and pure ; their v*.*nters are seldom subjest to frost or snow. When the former happens, it lafts not long ; and the latter never lies upon the ground. The heat of their summers is much abated by sea-breezes. They are indeed frequently incommoded by sea fogs, but these are not unwholesome. Agues are rare, and fevers more so. The most fatal distemper is the small-pox ; yet those who live temperately survive commonly to a great age, and are remarkably free from discases. The foil is very good, and produces grain of all forts (except wheat, of which they had anciently plenty) in large quantities. They still grow a little wheat, but the bread made of it is unpleasant. They eat, for this reason, chiefly what is made of barky ; and of this they have such abundance, that though they use it both for bread anpl beer, they have more than suffices for their own consumption. The use of potatoes is a new improvement ; and they prosper to such a degree, that in some places there are two crops in a-year. Roots of all forts, pulse, and salads, grow well ; dwarf fruit-trees, goofeberrfes, currants, raspberries, and ev^'ry thing of that kind, under proper shelter, thrive exceedingly ; but they have no trees, though formerly they had elder ; and porthelik, i. f. the harbour of willows, proves they had these likewise ; and wltl a little care, no doubt, great improvements might be made. The ranunculus, anemone, and most kinds of flowers, are successfully •cultivate^ their gardens. They have wild fowl of all

Ibrts, rom the swan to the snipe ; and 3 particular kind Si called the hedge chicken, which is not inferior to the oi town : also tame fowl, puffins, and rabbits, in great numb<;rs. Their black cattle are generally fr all, but very well tasted, though they feed upon ore -weed. Their horses are little, but strong and lively. They have also large flocks of ftne flieep, whose fleeces are tolerably good and their fief li excellent. There are no venomous creatures in these islands.

We reft now pass to the sea, which is of more consequence to these isles than that small portion of land which is distributed amongst them. St Mary's harbour is very safe and capacious, having that i(lai?!d on the south ; the eastern islands, with that of St Martin, on the east ; Trefcaw, Brehar, and Samson, to the north ; St Agnes and several small Islands to the weft. Ships ride here in three to five fathom water, with good anchorage. Into this harbour there are four inlets, viz. Broad Sound, Smith's Sound, St Mary's Sound, and Crow Sound : so that hardly any wind can blow with which a flip of 150 tons cannot safely fail through one or other of them. Crow Sound only excepted, where they cannot pass at low water, but at high there is from 16 to 24 feet in this passage. Besides these there are two other labours ; one called Netu Grynfey, which lies between Brehar and Trefcaw, where flu'ps of 300 tons may ride securely. The other is called Old Grynfey, and lies between Trefcaw, St Helen's, and Theon, for fern aller ships. The former is guarded by the batteries at OHver's Castle ; the latter by the Blockhouse, on the eastern side of Ire scow, called Donjer. Small coasters bound to the northward have more convenient outlets from these little harbours than from St Mary's, where, at the weft end of Hugh Town, there is a fine pier built by the present earl of Godolphin, 430 feet long, 20 feet wide in the narrowest part, and 23 feet in height, with 16 feet of water at a fpnng, and 10 at a neap tide ; so that under the flies ter of this pier, vessels of 150 tons may lie securely, not only close to the quay, but all along the strand of the town.

In this harbour, and in all the little coves of the several isles, prodigious quantities of mackerel may be caught in their season ; alf) foal, turbot, and plaise, remarkably good in their kind and ling, which from its being a thicker fissi, mellower, and better fed, is very justly preferred to any caught nearer our own coasts. Salinon, cod, pollock, are in great plenty, and pilchards in vast abundance. To these we may add the alga marina, fucus, or ore-weed, which serves to feed both their small and great cattle, manures their lands, is burned into kelp, is of use in physic, is sometimes preserved, sometimes pickled, and is in many other respects very beneficial co the inhabitants, of whom we are next to speak.

The people of Scilly in general are robust, handsome, active, hardy, industrious, generous, and good natured ; speak the English language with great propriety ; have strong natural parts (though for want of a good school they have little education), as appears by their dexterity in the several employments to which they are bred. They cultivate most of their lands as well as can be expected under their present circumstances. They are bred from their infancy to the management of their boats, in which they excel are good

mirable housewives, spin their own wool, weave it into coarse cloth, and knit slockings. They have uo timber of their own growth, and Jiot much from England ; yet they have many joiners and cabinet-makers, who, out of the fine woods which they obtain from captains of (hips who put in here, make all kinds of domestic furniture in a very neat manner. They trre free from the land-tax, malt-tax, and excise ; and being furuiflied with plenty of hquors from the vefftls which are driven mot their roads for refreshment, for necessary repairs, or to wait for a fair wind, in return for provisions and other conveniences ; this, with what little fish they can cure, makes the best part of their trade, if we except their kelp, which has been a growing manus adure for these fourscore years, and produces at present about cool, per annum. . n. i j

The right honourable the carl of Godolphm is Ityled proprietor of Scilly, in ^irtue of letters-patent granted to the late earl, then lord Godolphin, dated the 25th of July 1698, for the term of 89 years, to be computed from the end and expiration of a term of 50 years, granted to Francis Godolphin, Esq; by king Charles I.; that is, from the year 1709 to n^^, wiien his lease determines. In virtue fif this royal grant, his lordship is the sole owner of ail lands, houses, and tenements ; claims all the tithes, .not only of the fruits of the earth, but of nih taken at/ea and landed upon those premises; harbour-duties paid by (hips ; and one moiety of ^ the wrecks, the other belonging to the admiralty. There is only one ecclesia if ical person upon the islands, who resides at St Mary's, and vihts the other _ inhabited i.nands once a-year. But divine service is performed, and sermons read, every Sunday in the churches of those islands, by an honest layman appointed for that purpose ; and there are likewise church-wardens and overseers, regularly chosen in every parish. As to the civii government, it is administered by what is called the Courf of Twelve ; in which the commander in chief, the proprietor's agent, and the chaplain, have their feats in virtue of their offices : the other nine are chosen by the people. These decide, or rather compromise, all differences ; and punish small offences by fines, whippings, and the dr king-stool : as to greater enormities, we many conclude they have not been hhlierto known ; since, except for the soldiers, there is no prison in the islands. But in cafe of capital ©fences, the criminals may be transported to the county of Cornwall, and there brought to justice.

The great importance of these islands arises from their advantageous situation, as looking equally into ^ George's Channel, which divides Great Britain from Ireland, and the English Channel, which separates Britain from France. For this reason, most flips bound from the southward strive to make the Scilly islands, in ©rder to fleer their course with greater certainty. It is very convenient also tor vessels to take flicker amongst them ; which, prevents their being driven to Milford Haven, nay sometimes into some port in Ireland, if the wind is strong at east ; or, if it blows hard at northwest , from being forced back into some of the Cornifli harbours,, or even on the French coasts. If the wind should not be very high, yet it unfavourable or unsteady, as between the channels often happens, it is better to jput into Scilly, than to beat about at sea in bad weather.

" It is a circumstance (says he) well known to seamen, 'that flips, in coming from the Atlantic, and fleering a course for the Britlfli channel, in a parallel somewhat to the south of the Scilly islands, do notwithstanding often find themselves to the north ©f those islands; or, in other words, in the mouth of St George's or of the Bristol channel. This extraordinary error has passed for the effects either of bad steerage, bad observations of latitude, or the indiuught of the Bristol channel: but none of these account for it satisfactorily ; because, admitting that at times there may be an indraught, it cannot be supposed to extend to Scilly ; and the cafe has happened in weather the most favourable for navigating and for taking observations. The consequences of this deviation from the intended trad have very often been fatal ; particularly in the loss of the Nancy packet in our own times, and that of Sir Cloudefley Shovel and others of his fleet at the beginning of the present century. Numbers of cases, equally melancholy, but of lefs celebrity, have occurred; and many others, in which the danger has been imminent, but not fatal, have scarcely reached the public ear. " I am, however, of opinion, that, they may be imputed to a specific cause; namely, a current: and I fliall therefore endeavouito investigate both that and its effects, that seamen may be apprized of the times when they are particularly to exped. it in any considerable: degree of ftrcligth ; for then only it is likely to occasion mischief, the current that prevails at ordinary times being probably too weak to produce an error in the reckoning, equal to the difference of parallel between the south part, of Scilly and the trad in which a commander, prudent in his measures, but unsuspicious of a current, would choose to fail."

SCITAMIN£^. See Botany, p. 459. SCIURUS, the SQUIRREL ; a genus of quadrupeds 'feelongingto the order of gllres. It has two fore-teeth in each jaw, the superior ones shaped like wedges, and the inferior ones compressed. There are l i species ; •of which the most remarkable are,

I. The vulgaris, or common squirrel, with ears terminated with long tufts of hair ; large, lively, black eyes ; head, body, legs, and tail, of a bright reddiOi brown ; breast and bell^' white ; hair on each side the tail lies flat. In Sweden and Lapland, it changes m V'intet into grey. In RufTia it is sometimes found black, in many parts of Er.gland there is a beautiful variety, with milk white tails. — This species inhabits Europe and North America, tile northern and the temperate parts of Asia : and a variety is even found as far south as the isle of Ceylon. It is a neat, lively, aftive animal; lives always in woods : in the spring, the female is seen pursued from tree to tree by the males, feigning an escape from their embraces ; makes its nest of moss and dried leaves l>between the fork of two branches ; brings three or four young at a time ; has two holes to its Deft ; stops up that on the side the wind blows, as Pliny justly remarks ; lays in a hoard of winter provision, such as nuts, acorns, &c. ; in summer, feeds on buds and young shoots ; is particularly fond of those of fir, and the young cones ; fits up to eat, and uses its forefeet as hands ; covers itself with its tail ; leaps to a surprising distance; when disposed to cross a river, apiece of bark is its boat, its tail the fail ; is in great plenty in Dunmallet, and there called Conn. ^ Boys frequently nurse this beautiful and aftive animal under cats.

There are three creatures, the squirrel, the fieldmouse, and the bird called the nuthatchy which live much on hazel nuts ; and yet they open them each in a different way. The first, after rasping off the small end, splits the shell in two with his long fore-teeth, as a man does with his knife ; the second nibbles a hole with his teeth, so regular as if drilled with a wimble, and yet so small, that one would wonder how the ke reel can be extra ded through it j while th€ last pecks

an ir regular ragged hole with its bill; but as tins arScli tift has no paws to hold the nut firm whil<; he pierces ""^ it, like an adroit workman, he fixes it, as it were in a vice, in some cleft of a tree, or in some crevice ; when, {landing over it, he perforates the stubborn fliell. They are very jnunerous in North America, do incredible damage to the plantations of maize, rim up

the stalks and eat the young ears. Descend in all locks from the mountains, and join those that inhabit the lower parts; are proscribed by the provinces, and a reward of three-pence per head given for every one that is killed. Such a number was destroyed one year, that Pennsylvania alone paid in rewards L. 8000 of its currency. Make their nefts in hollow trees, with moss, straw, w^ool, &c. Feed on maize in the season, and on pine-cones, acorns, and m^fts of all kinds : form holes under-ground, and there deposit a large flock of winter provision. Descend from the trees, and visit their magazines when in want of meat ; are particularly busy at the approach of bad weather ; during the cold season keep in their nest for several days together ; seldom leap from tree to tree, only run up and down the bodies ; their hoards often destroyed by swine ; when their magazines are covered with deep iiaow, the squirrels often perish for want of food ; are not easily (hot, nimbly changing their place when they fee the gun levelled ; have the aftluns of the common squirrel ; are easily ta^ med ; and their flesh is esteemed very delicate. Their furs, which arc imported under the name of petii-grist are valuable, and used as linings to cloaks.

3. The filler, or black squirrel, with plain cars j sometimes wholly black, but often marked with white on the nose, the neck, or end of the tail ; the tail shorter than that of the former ; the body equal. It inhabits the north of Asia, North America, and Mexi. CO ; breeds and associates in separate troops ; is equally numerous , with the former; commits as great ravages among the maize ; makes its nest in the same manner, and forms, like them, magazines for wren ter food. The finest are taken near the lake Baikal, and about Bargu2inst<oi-Gftrog, upon the Upper Angara, in the diftridil of Nertfchinflc, which are the best in all Siberia; these continue black the w^hole year, the others grow rusty in summer. — There is a variety with plain ears ; coarse fur mixed with dirty white and black ; throat and inside of the legs and thighs black ; tail much shorter than those of squirrels usually are ; of a dull yellow colour, mixed with black ; body of the size of the giey squirrel. It inhabits Virginia ; the planters call it the cat squirrel.

4. i'he Slav suf or fair squirrel, with the body and tail of a flaxen colour; of a very small size, with plain round

' ears, and rounded tail. Inhabits the woods near Amadabad, the capital of Guzurat, in great abundance, leap., ing from tree to tree. Linnaeus fays it. is an inhabitant of South America.

5. The Jirtatusy or ground squirrel, with plain ears ;

• ridge of tlie back marked with a black streak ; each side with a pale yellow stripe, bounded above and below with a line of black ; head, body, and tail, of a reddish brown ; the tail the darkest : breast and belly white ; noie and feet pale-red ; eyes full. — Inhabits the north of Asia, but found in the greatest abundance in the forests of North America. They never run up trees except they are pursued, and find no other means of escaping : they but row, and form their habitations under ground, with two entrances, that they - may get access to the one in cafe the other is flopped up. Their retreats are formed with great skill, in form of a long gallery, with branches on each side, each of which terminates in an enlarged chamber, as a magazine to store their winter provision in ; in one they lodge the acorns, in another the maize, in a third the hickory nuts, and in the last their save urite food the chinquapin chesnut. They very seldom stir out during winter, at least as long as their provisions last ; but if that fails, they will dig into cellars \. here apples are kept, or barns where maize is stored, and do a great deal of mischief ; but at that time the cat destroys great numbers, and is as great an enemy to them as to mice. During the maize harvest these squirrels are very busy in biting off the ears, and filling their mouths so full with th^ corn, that their cheeks are quite distended. It is observable that they give great preference to certain food ; for if, after filling their mouths with rye, they happen to meet with wheat, they fling away the first, that they may indulge in the last. They are very wild, bite severely, and are scarcely ever tamed ; the ficins are of little use, but are sometimes brought over to line cloaks.

It was esteemed a great delicacy by the Romans, who had their gliraria, places constructed to keep and feed them in.

The arquatay or curlew, frequents our sca-coast and marshes in the winter time in large flocks, walking on the open fands ; feeding on shells, frogs, crabs, and other marine infefts. lu summer they retire to the mountainous and unfrequented parts of the country, where they pair and breed. Their eggs are of a pale olive colour, marked with irregular but distinct spots of pale brown. Their flesh is very rank and fishy, notwithstanding an old English proverb in its favour. Curlews differ much in weight and size ; some welqrhing 37 ounces, others not 22: the length of the largest to the tip of the tail, 25 inches ; the breadth, three feet five inches ; the bill is seven inches long : the head, neck, and coverts of the wings are of a pale brown ; the middle of each feather, black ; the breast and belly white, marked with narrow oblong black lines : the back is white, spotted with a few black strokes : the quill feathers are black, but the' inner webs spotted with white ;• the tail is white, tinged with red, and beautifully barred with black ; the" legs are Ion;, strong, and of a bluish grey colour ; the bottoms of the toes flat and broad, to enable it to walk on the soft mud, in search of food.

2. The phanpus, or whimbrel, is much less frequent on our {hores than the curlew ; but its haunts, food, and general appearance, are much the same. It is observed to visit the neighbour hood of Spalding (where it is called the curse iv knot) in vast flocks ir> April, but continues there no longer than May ; nor is it seen there any other time of the year : it seems at that season to be on its passage to its breeding place, which Mr Pennant suspects to be among the Highlands of Scotland. The specific dill"erence is the size ; this never exceeding the weight of 1 2 ounces.

3. The rusty cola, or woodcock, during summer inhabits the Alps of Norway, Sweden, Polifli Prussia, the march of Brandenburg, and the northern parts of Europe : they all retire from those countries the beginning of winter, as soon as the frosts commence ; which force them into milder climates, where the ground is open, and adapted to their manner of feeding. They live on worms and infefts, whidi they search for with their long bills in soft grounds and moist woods. — Woodcocks generally arrive here in flocks, taking advantage of the night or a mill: : they soon separate ; but before they return to their native haunts, pair. They feed and fly by night ; beginning their slight in the evening, and return the same way or through the same glades to their day retreat. They leave England the latter end of February, or beginning of March ; not but they have been known to continue here accidentally. These birds appear in Scotland first: on the eastern coast:s, and make their progress from east; to weft. They <so not arrive in Breadalljane, a central part of the kingdom, till the beginning or middle of November ; nor the coasts of Nether Lorn, or of Rofslhire, till Dei-ember or January : they are very rare in fhe remote Hebrides, and in the Orkneys. A few stragglers now and then arrive there. They are equally scarce in Calthnefs. Our species of woodcock is unknown in

• North America : but a kind is found that has the gener'" %i\ appearance of it ; but is scarce half the size, and wants the bars on the breast and belly. The weight of the woodcock is usually about 12 ounces; the length near 14 inches ; and the breadth, 26 j the bill is three

The male is diftinguiflicd from the female by some black lines on the breast and throat ; which in the female are wanting. These birds are taken in the fens, in the same season and in the same manner with the ruffs and reeves * ; and when fattened are • Sea esteemed a great delicacy, and fell for half a crown or '^"'i five fliiUings a piece. A stale of the same species is placed in the net. They appear in small flocks on our coasts in September, and continue with us the whole winter ; they walk on the open fands like the curlew^ and feed on insects

5. The glottis y or green flank, is in length to the end of the tail, 1 4 inches ; to that of the toes, 20 ; it& breadth, 25. The bill is two inches and a half long ; the upper mandible black, straight, and very slender ; the lower reflects a little upwards; the head and upper part of the neck are ash-coloured, marked with small dusky lines pointing down; over each pastes a white line ; the coverts, the scapulars, and upper part of the back, are of a brownish assi-colour ; the quill-feathers dust ley, but the inner webs speckled with white ; the breast, belly, thighs, and lower part oi the back, are white ; the tail is white, marked with undulated dust ley bars : the inner coverts of the wings finely crofTed with double and treble rows of a dust ley colour. It is a bird of an elegant shape, and small weight in proportion to its dimensions, weighing only six ounces. The legs are very long and slender, and bare above two inches higher than the knees. he exterior toe is united to the middle toe, as far as the Cecond joint, by a strong

6. The calid rist or red-shank, is found on most of our (hores ; in the winter time it conceals itself in the gutters, and is generally found single or at most in pairs. It breeds in the fens and madhes ; and flies round its nest when diilurbed, makmg a noise like a lapwing. It lays four eggs, whitish tinged with olive, marked with irregular spots of black chiefly on the thicker end. It weighs five ounces and a half : the length is 1 2 inches, the breadth 2 1 ; the bill near two inches long, red at the base, black towards the point. The head, hind part of the neck, and scapulars, are of a dufl<y a(colour, obscurely spotted with black; the back is white, sprinkled with black spots; the tail elegantly barred with black and white ; the cheeks, under side of the neck, and upper part of the breast, are white, streaked downward with dusky Hnes ; the belly white ; the exterior webs of the quill feathers are diiflcy ; the legs long, and of a fine bright orange colour ; the utmost toe connected to the middle toe by a small membrane ; the inmost by another still smaller.

7. The galUnagOy or common snipe, weighs four •unces ; the length, to the end of the tail, is near 1 2 inches j the breadth about 14 ; the bill is three inches long, of a dusky colour, flat at the end, and often rough like rtiagrin above and below. The head is divided seng^th wife with two black lines, and three of red, one of the last passing over the middle of the head, and one above each eye: between the bill and the eyes is a dust ley line ; the chin is white ; the neck is varied with brown and red. The scapulars are beautifully fl;riped lengvhwife with black and yellow ; the quill-feathers are -dust ley ; but the edge of the first is white, as are the tips of the secondary feathers : the quill-feathers next the back are barred with black and pale red ; the breast and belly are white; the coverts of the tail are long, and almost cover it; they are of a reddish brown colour. The -tail consists of ; 4 feathers, black on their lower part, then crofted with a broad bar of deep orange, another narrow one of black ; and the ends white, or pale orange. The vent feathers are of a dull yellow ; the legs pale green; the toes divided to their origin. In the winter-time snipes are very frequent in all our mar fly and wet grounds, where they lie concealed in the Tufties, &c. In summer they disperse to different parts, and are foimd in the midst of our highest mountains as well as of our low moors ; their nest is made of dried grass ; they lay four eggs of a dirty olive colour, marked with dust ley spots ; their young are so often found in England, that we doubt whether they ever entirely leave this island. When they are disturbed much, particularly in the breeding season, they soar to a vast height, making a Angular bleating noise ; and when they descend, dart down with vast rapidity : it is also amusing to observe the cock, while his mate fits on her

^eggs, poise himself on her wings, making sometimes a •whistling and sometimes a drumming noise. Their food is the same with that of the woodcock ; their slight very ' irregular apd swift, and attended with a ftiriU scream. They are most universal birds, found in every quarter of the globe, and in all climates.

The scolopendra is also called the centipees from its number of feet. In the Eafl: Indies it grows to fix inches in length, and as thick as a man's finger : it consists of many joints ; and from each joint proceeds a leg on each side : they are covered with hair, and seem to have no eyes ; but there are two feelers on the head, with which they find out the way they are to pass : the head is very round, with two small sharp teeth, with which they inst id wounds that are very painful and dangerous. A sailor that was bit by one on board a flip felt excessive pain, and his life was supposed to be in danger ; but by the application of roasted onions to the part he recovered. The bite of the scolopendra morjitans § in Jamaica is § See Plate said to be as poisonous as the sting of a scorpion.- " Some of the species live in holes in the earth : others under stones, and among rotten wood ; so that the removing of these is exceedingly dangerous in the countries where the scolopendrae breed. — These infefts, like the scorpion, are supposed to be produced persed from the parent or the egg, and to^ undergo no changes after their first exclusion. They are found of all fizes ; which is a sufficient reason for believing that they preserve their first appearance through the whole of their existence. It is probable, however, that, like most of this class, they often change their flcins j but of this we have no certain information. The scolopendra forficata is the largest in this country, of a dun colour, smooth, and composed of nine scaly segments, without reckoning the head. The feet are 15 in number on each side, and the last longer than the reft> and turned backwai ds, form a kind of forky tail. The ante nine are twice the length of the head, and consist of 42 short segments. The infed's progressive motion is very quick, and sometimes serpentine. It is found under stones on the ground, under flower-pots and garden boxes.

SCOMBER, the Mackerel, in ichthyology, a genus belonging to the order of thoracic. The head is smooth and compressed, and there are seven rays in the gill membrane. There are ten species; — of which the most remarkable are the following.

I . The scomber, or common mackerel, a summer-fith of passage that visits our ftiores in vast flo als. It Is less useful than other species of gregarious fish, being very tender, and unfit for carriage ; not but that it may be preserved by pickling and faking, a method, we believe, praiSliied only In Cornwall, where It proves a great relief to the poor during winter. It was a sisti greatly ■esteemed by the Romans, because It furnished the preclous garum, a sort of pickle that gave a high relicti to their fauces ; and was besides used medicinally. It was drawn from different kinds of hili, but that made from the mackerel had the preference : the best was made • at 4X2 . CarSCO [ yi

Scomber. Carthagena, vast quantities of mackerel being taken near fc— V "■' an adjacent isle, called from that circumstance Scornbrarla, and the garum, prepared by a certain company in that city, bore a high price, and was dillinguiflied by the title of garum fociorum. This fish is easily taken by a bait ; but the best time is during a fret li gale of wind, which is thence called a mackerel gale. In the spring the eyes of mackerel ^re almost covered with a white film ; during which period they are half blind. This film grows in winter, and is call the beginning of summer. It is not often that it exceeds two pounds in weight, yet there have been instances of some that weighed upwards of five. Tlie nose is taper and (harp pointed ; the eyes large ; the jaws of an equal length ; the teeth small, but numerous. The form of this fish is very elegant. The body is a little compressed on the fides : towards the tail it grows very slender, and a little angular. It is a most beautiful fissi when have ; for nothing can equal the brilliancy of its colour, which death impairs, but does not wholly obliterate.

2. The thunnus, or tunny, was a fish well known to the ancients : it made a considerable branch of commerce : the time of its arrival in the Mediterranean from the ocean was observed, and stations for taking them were established in places it most frequented.

There are still very confiderable tunny fisher les on the coast of Sicily, as well as several other parts of the Mediterranean ; where they are cured, and make a great article of provision in the adjacent kingdoms.— They are caught in nets, and amazing quantities are taken ; fer they come in vast flo als, keeping along the shores. See Tunny-Fisher. ,

They frequent our coasts, but not in Ihoals hke the tunnies of the Mediterranean. They are not uncommon in the lechs on the western coast of Scotland ; where they come in pursuit of herrings ; and often during night strike into the nets, and do confiderable dar mage. When the fishermen draw them up in the mornr ing, the tunny rises at the same time towards the surface, ready to catch the fi(h that drop out. Om perceiving it, a strong hook baited with a herring, and fastened to a rope, is instantly flung out, which the tunny seldom fails to take. As soon as hooked, it loses all spirit ;.and after a very little resistance submits to its fate. It is dragged to the ftiore and cut up, either to be sold fresh to people who carry it to the country markets, or is preserved salted in large basis. The pieces, when fresh,. look, exactly like raw beef ; but when boiled turn pale, and have something of the flavour of salmon.

One that was taken when Mr Pennant was at Inverary in 1769, weighed 460 pounds. The fissi was seven feet ten Inches, long : , the greatest circumference five feet seven ; the ieast near the tall one foot six. The body was rouiul and thick, and grew suddenly very {lender towards the tail, and near that part was angular. The irides were of a plain green :. the teeth very minute. The tall was in form of a crescent ; and two feet seven inches between tip and tip. The flcin on the back was smooth, very thick, and black. On the belly the scales were visible. The colour of the fides and belly was silvery, tinged with cjerulean and pale purple : near the tail marbled with grey..

scone.c:
SCONE, a town of Scotland, remarkable for being the place where the kings were anciently crowned. W. Long. 3. 10. N. Lat. 56. 28. Here was once an abbey of great antiquity, which was burnt by the reformers at Dundee. Kenneth II. upon his conquest of the Pids in the ninth century, having made Scone his principal residence, delivered his laws, called the Macalpine laws, from a tumulus, named the Mote Hill of Scone. The present palace was begun by the earl of Gowrie ; but was completed by Sir David Murray of Gofpatrie, the save urite of king James VI. to whom that monarch had granted it ; and the new possessor in gratitude to his benefactor put up the king's arms in several parts of the house. It is built around two courts. The dining room is large and handsome ; and has an ancient and magnificent chimney-piece, and the king's arms, with this motto :

Nobis htec inviSa mise runt centum sex proa vt. .

Beneath are the Murray arms. In the drawing room ■: is some good old tapestry, with an excellent figure of mercury. In a small bed-chamber is a medley scripture-place in needle-work, with -a border of animals,, pretty well done, the work of queen Mary during her confinement in Loch Leven Castle. The gallery is about 155 feet long, the top arched, divided int© compartments filled with paintings in water-colours. The pieces represented are various kinds of huntings ; that of Nimrod, ,and king James and his train, appear ia every piece. Till the destruction of the abbey, the kings of Scotland were crowned here, fitting in the famous wooden chair which Edward I. transported to Weftmlnfter abbey, to the great mortification of the Scots, who looked upon it as a kind of palladium. Charles II. before the battle of Worcester, was crowned in the present chapel. Scorpana is also the name of a fish caught in many parts of the Mediterranean. It seldom grows to more than a pound weight. Its body is long, but not flatted, and is moderat ely thick. Its head is extremely large, and is armed with prickles, and it grows gradually less from thence to the tail. The prickles about the head are accounted venomous, and the fi/her men usually cut them off as feon as the fish is caught. Its tail is not forked, but rounded at the end. Of all the classes of noxious infefts the scorpion is the most terrible, whose fliape is hideous, whose size among the inst cas is enormous, and whose fling is generally fatal. Happy for Britain, the scorpion is entirely a stranger among; us ! In several parts of the continent of Europe it is Ibut too well known, though it seldom grows above four inches long : but in the warm tropical climates, it is seen a foot in length, and in every respect as large as a lobster, which it somewhat resembles in (hape. There have been enumerated nine different kinds of this dangerous inst del, including species and varieties, chiefly distinguished by their colour ; there being scorpions yellow, brown, and assi-coloured ; others that are the colour _of rufl;y iron, green, pale yellow, black, claret colour, white, and grey. There are four principal parts dist^ingulf liable in this animal ; the head, the b roast, the belly, and the tall. The fcorplon's head fee-ms, as it were, jointed to the breast ; in the middle of which are seen two eyes ; and a little more forward, two eyes more, placed in the fore part of the head: those eyes are so small, tliat they are scarcely parcel warble ; and it is probable the animal has but Title occafiion for seeing. The mouth is farnllTied with two jaws : the undermost is divided into two, and the parts notched into each other, which serves the animal as teeth, and with which it breaks its . food, and thruils it intO) its mouth : these the scorpion can at pleasure pull hack into its mouth, so. that no part of them can be se en. On each side - of the head are two arms, each composed of four joints ; the sail of which is large, with il rong muscles, and made in the raannsr of a lobiler's claw. Below the breail ale eight, articulated legs, each divided into six joints ; the two hindmost of which are eacli provided with two crooked claws, and here and. there covered with hair. The belly is divided into seven little rings ; frum the lovvcH

of which is continued a tail, composed of six joints, Scorpio, which are bristly, and formed hke little globes, the last being armed with a crooked sting. This is that fatal instrument which renders this infeft so formidable : it is long, pointed, hard, and hollow ; it is pierced near the base by two small holes, through which, when the animal stings, it ejects a drop of poison, which is white, caustic, and fatal. The reservoir in which this poison is kept, is in a small bladder near the tall, into which the venom is distilled by a peculiar apparatus. If this bladder be greatly pressed, the venom will be seen issuing out through the two holes above-mentioned ; so that it appears, that when the animal stings, the bladder is pressed, and the venom issues through the two apertures into the wound.

We have here given the common account of the sting of these noxieus animals ; but though we cannot pretend to determine between them, we fliall lay before our readers the following observations from a treatise on Troitcal Diseases, &c. by Dr Moseley of the Chelsea Hospital. " Galen justly observes, that a person who had not witnessed the fast, would not suppose that so small an injury as the sting of a scorpion, or the bite of a poisonous spider, could produce the violent effects which they do in the whole body. He says, the aculeus, or sting, of a scorpion ends in the minutest point ; and has no perforation through which any poison can pass into the wound. Yet, he says, we must suppose the venom to be some spirit al substance, or moisture, iii which a great power is concentrated in a small compass. Before I had an opportunity (fays Dr Moseley) of examining this subjest, my respect for the opinion of Galen made me doubt the accuracy of Leeuwenhoekj Redi, Mead, and others, who assert that there is aa aperture i^ear the cuspis of a fcorpion's sting ; and that through this aperture a liquid poison is injeded when a wound is inflidled. Repeated experiments, with the best glasses, have never enabled me to discover any foramen, or opening, whatever."

There are few animals more formidable, or more truly mischievous, than the scorpion. As it takes refuge in a small .place, and is generally found flieh , tering in houses, it must frequently sting those among*

In some of the towna of Italy, ■~v~-- and in France, in the province of Languedoc, it is one of the greatest pests that torments mankind ^ but its malignity in Europe is trifling, when coin pared to what the natives of Africa and the east are known to experience. In Batavia, where they grow twelve inches long, there is no removing any piece of furniture, without the utmost danger of being stung by them. Bofman assures us, that along the Gold Coast they are often found larger than a lobster ; and that their sting is inevitably fatal. In Europe, however, they are by no means so large, so venomous, or so numerous, 'i he general frae of this animal does not exceed two or three inches ; and its sting is very seldom found to be fatal. Maupertius, who made several experiments on the scorpion of Languedoc, found it by uo means so invariably dangerous as had till then been represented. He provoked one of them to sting a dog, in three places of the belly where the animal was without hair. In about an hour after, the poor animal seemed greatly R. olsen, -aad became very fick ; he then call up whatever he had in his bowels; and for about three hours continued vomiting a whitish liquid. The belly was always greatly two ven when the animal began to vomit ; but this operation always seemed to abate the swelling,; which alternately swelled, and was thus emptied, for three hours successively. The poor animal after this fell into convulsions, bit the ground, dragged himself along upon his fore-feet, and at last died, Hve hours after being bitten. He was not partially two ven round the place which was bitten, as is usual after the sting of a wasp or a bee ; but his whole body was inflated, and there only appeared a red spot on the places where he had been stung.

Some days after, however, the same experiment was tried upon another dog, and even with more aggravated cruelty : yet the dog seemed no way affected by the wounds: but, howling a little when he received them, • continued alert and well after them ; and soon after was set at liberty, without showing the smallest symptoms of pain. So far was this poor creature from being terrified at the experiment, that he left his own maftei's house, to come to that of the philosopher, where he had received more plentiful entertainment. The same experiment was tried by fresh fcoi-pious upon seven other dogs, and upon three hens ; but not the smallest deadly symptom was seen to ensue. From hence it appears, that many circumstances, which are utterly unknown, Tnuft contribute to give efficacy to the fcorpion's venom. Whether its food, long tasting, the season, the nature of the vessels it wounds, or its state of maturity, contribute to or retard its malignity, is yet to be ascertained by succeeding experiment. In the trials made by our philosopher, he employed, scorpions of both fexes, newly caught, and seemingly vigorous and aftive. The success of this experiment may serve to shew, that many of those boasted antidotes which are given for the cure of the fcorpion's sting, owe their success rather to accident than their own efficacy. They only happened ^o cure when then' sting was no way dangerous ; but in cases of actual malignity, they might probably be utterly unserviceable

The scorpion of the tropical climates being much larger than the former, is probably much more vena- .tnous. Helbigius, however, who refused for many years

in ths east, assures m, that he was often stung by the ■ scorpion, and never received any material injury from - the wound : a painfd tumor generally ensued 5 but he always cured it by rubbing th=e part with a piece of iron or stone, as he bad seen the Indians practise before him, until the fief ii became insensible, Seba, Moore, and Bofman, however, give a very different account of the fcorpion's malignity : and assert, that, unless speedily relieved, the wound becomes fatal.

It is certain, that no animai in the creation seems endued with such an irascible nature. They have often been seen, when taken and put into a place of security, to exert all their rage against the fides of the glass-vessel that contained them. They will attempt to sting a stick when put near them ; and attack a mouse or a frog, while those animals are far from offering any injury. Maupertius put three scorpions and a mouse in-^ to the same vestel together, and they soon stung the little animal in different places. The mouse, thus assaulted, stood for some time upon the defensive, and at last killed them all, ©ne after another. He tried this experiment, in order to see whether the mouse, after it had killed, would eat the scorpions ; but the little quadruped seemed satisfied with the vlftory, and even survived the severity of the wounds it had received. Wolkamer tried the courage of the scorpion against the large spider, and inclosed several of both kinds in glass vessels for that purpose. The success of this combat was very remarkable. The spider at first used all its efforts to intangle the scorpion in its web, which it immediately began spinning ; but the scorpion rescued itself from the danger, by flinging its adversary to death 4 it soon after cut off, with its claws, all the legs of the spider, and then sucked all the internal parts at its leisure. — If the fcorpion's skin had not been so hard, Wolkamer is of opinion that the spider would have obtained the victory ; for he had often seen one of these spiders destroy a toad.

The fierce spirit of this animal is equally dangerous to its own species ; for scorpions art the cruellefl enemies to each other. Maupertius put about 100 of therri together in the same glass ; and they scarce came into conta6l when they began to exert all their rage in mutual destruction : there was nothing to be seen but one universal carnage, without any distinction of age or sex ; so that in a few days there remained only 14, which had killed and devoured all the reft.

But their unnatural malignity is still more' apparent in their cruelty to their offspring. He inclosed a female scorpion, big with young, in a glass vessel, and (he was seen to devour them as fast as they were excluded ; there was but one only of the number that escaped the general destruction, "by taking refuge on the back of its parent ; and this soon after revenged the cause of its brethren, by killing the old one in its turn.

Such is the terrible and unrelenting nature of this inst del, which neither tlie bonds of society nor of nature can reclaim : it is even asse ited, that, when driven to an extremity, the scorpion will often destroy itself. The following experiment was ineffeftuaUy tried by Maupertius: " But," says Mr Goldsmith, " I am so well assured of it by many eye-witnesses, who have seen it both in Italy and America, that I have no doubt remaining of its veracity. A scorpion, newly caught,

orplo, 18 placed in the midst of a circle of burning charcoal, piurus. ^Ij^jg egress prevented on every side ; the scarp ton, as I am assured, runs for about a minute round the circle, in hopes of escaping : but finding that impossible, it stings itself on the back of the head ; and in this manner the undaunted suicide instantly expires."

It is happy for mankind that these animals are thus dettrucSlive to each other ; since otherwise they would multiply in so great a degree as to render feme countries uninhabitable. The male and female of this infeft are very easily distinguishable ; the male being smaller and less hairy. The female brings forth her young alive, and perfe6l in their kind. Redi having bought a quantity of scorpions, selected the females, which, by their size and roughness were easily distinguishable from the reft, and putting them in separate glass vessels, he kept them for some days without food. In about five days one of them brought forth 38 young ones, well iii aped, and of a milk-white colour, which changed eveiy day more and more into a dark rusty hue. Another female, in a different vessel, brought forth 27 of the same colour ; and the day following the young ones seemed all fixed to the back and belly of the female. For near a fortnight all these continued alive and well : but afterwards some of them died daily ; until, in about a month, they all died except two.

Were it worth the trouble, these animals, mi^ht be kept living as long as curiosity should think proper. Their chief food is worms and infefts ; and upon a proper supply of these, their lives might be lengthened to their natural extent. How long that may be, we are not told ; but if we may argue from analogy, it cannot be less than seven or eight years ; and perhaps, in the larger kind, double that duration. As they have somewhat the form of the lobfl;er, so they resemble that animal in calling their shell, or more properly their plain ; since it is fofter by far than the covering of the lobiler, and set with hairs, which grow from it in great abundance, particularly at the joinings. The young lie in the womb of the parent, each covered up in its own membrane, to the number oi 40 or 50, and united to each other by an oblong thread, so as to exhibit altogether the form of a chaplet.

Such is the manner in which the common scorpion produces its young-: but there is a scorpion of America

Produced from the egg, in the manner of the spider. "lie eggs are no longer than pins points; and they axe deposited in a web, which they spin from their bodies, and carry about with them, till they are hatched. As soon as the young ones are excluded from the shell, they get upon the hack of the parent, who turns her tail over them, and defends them with her fiing. It seems probable, therefore, that captivity produces that unnatural disposition in the scorpion which induces it to destroy its young ; since, at liberty, it is found to protest them with such unceasing assiduity. For the various modes of preventing the fatal consequences of the bites of these and other noxious animals, we refer to Mofeley's treatise above quoted.

Nova SCOTIA, or New Scotland, one of the British settlements in North America, situated between 43° and 49^ north latitude, and between 60" and 67^ weft longitude, is bounded by the river St Saurence on the north ; by the gulph of St Saurence and the Atlantic ocean on the east ; by the same ocean on the south ; and by Canada and New England on the weft. — In the year 1784, this province was divided into two governments. The province and government now ^y\t6.Neiv Brvnfwlck is bounded on the w^eft ward of the mouth of the river St Croix, by the said river to its source, and by a line drawn due north from thence to the southern boundary of the province of Quebec, to the northward by the said boundary as far as the western extremity of the Bay de Chaleurs, to the eastward by the said bay to the gulph of St I^our ence to the bay called Bay Verte, to the south by a Irne in the centre of the Bay of Fundy, from the river St Croix aforesaid, to the m.south of the Mufquat river, by the said river to its source, and from thence by a due east line across the Tfthmus into the Bay Verte, to join the eastern lot above described, including all islands within six leagues of the coast.

The chief rivers are, the river of St Saurence, which forms the northern boundary. The rivers Rifgouche and Nipifiguit run from weft to east, and fall into the bay of St Saurence. The rivers of St John, PafTariiagn ;di, Penobscot} aud St Croix, which rua from

north to south, fall Into-Fundy Bay, or the sea a little Nova to the eastward of it. Scotia,

The seas adjoining to it are, the Atlantic ocean, * Fundy Bay, and the gulph of St Saurence. The lesser bays are, Ghenigto and Green Bay upon the isthmus which joins the north part of Nova Scotia to the south ; and the Bay of Chaleurs on the north-east ; the Bay of Chcdibufto on the south-east ; the Bay of the Islands, the Ports of Bart, Chebuao, Prosper, St Margaret, La Heve, port Maltois, port Rylignol, port Vert, and port Joly, on the south ; port La Tour on the south east ; port St Mary, Anapolis, and Minas on the south side of Fundy Bay, and port Rofeway, now the most populous of all. — The chief capes are, Cape Portage, Ecoumenac, Tourmentin, Cape Port, and Epis, on the east ; Cape Fogerie and Cape Canceau on the south-east ^ Cape Blanco, Cape Vert, Cape Theodore, Cape Dore, Cape La Heve, and Cape Negro, on the south ; Cape Sable and Cape Fourche on the southwest. — The lakes are very numerous, but have not yet received particular names.

The face of the country, when viewed at a distance, presents a pleasingly variegated appearance of hills and valleys, with scarcely any thing like mountains to interrupt the prospect, especially near the sea. A nearer approach discovers those sublime and beautiful scenes which are so far superior to the gaudy embelliftiments of art. Immense forests, formed of the talleft trees, the growth of ages, and reaching almost to the clouds," everywhere cover and adorn the land : Their leaves falling in autumn, add continually to that crust of mofs, vegetables, and decaying wood, that ha« for many centuries been accumulating ; whilst the rays of the sun, unable to pierce the thick {hade which everywhere covers the ground, leaves it in a perpetual state of damp and rottenness ; a circumstance which contributes, in no small degree, to increase the flier press of the air in winter.

The clouds, ^ying over the higher grounds, which are covered in every direction with one vast forest, and arrested by the attraction of the woods, fill the country with water. Every rock has a spring, and every spring caufes a swamp or morass, of greater or less extent in proportion to its cause : hence it is, that travelling becomes almost impracticable in summer, and is seldom attempted, but in the fall of the year, when winter begins to set in, and the ground is already frozen.

The land throughout the peninsula is in no part mountainous, but frequently rises into hills of gradual ascent, everywhere clothed with wood. From these arise innumerable springs and rivulets, which not only fertilize and adorn the country, but have formed, in the midst of it, a large lake or piece of fret ti water, which is of various depths, and of which, however, little more is known, than that it has upon its borders very large tradls of meadow-land highly improveable. That part of the province which is beyond the Bay of Fundy, and extends to the river St Saurence, rifes also gradually as we advance from the sea quite to Canada, but is, however, hardly anywhere mountainous. Its lands, are for the most part very rich, particularly at a distance from the sea ; and its woods abound with the hardest and loft left trees.

Though this country, like Canada, is fubjed to long

and

SCO I 7

and fevers winters, succeeded by sudden and violent heats, often much greater than what are felt in the same latitudes in Europe, yet It cannot be accounted an unhealthy climate. The air in j^cneral In winter is very sharp. frosty, and drf ; the fl:y serene and uncloi;ded, by which every kind of exercise adapted to the season is rendered pltalaiit and ap.reeable. The fogs are frequent near the sea, but seldom spread themselves to any distance in land.

The winter commonly breaks up with heavy rains, and the inhabitant* experience hardly any of the delights of the sprin?, which in England is accounted the most agreeable season of the year. From a lifeless and dreary appearance, and the bloody scenes of winter wrapped around the vegetable world, the countrythrows off its disgustful attire, and in a few days exhibits a grand and pleasant prospect ; the vegetation being inconceivably rapid, nature passes suddenly from one extreme to another, in a manner utterly unknown to countries accwftomed to a gradual progression of seasons. And, strange as it may appear, it Is an acknowledged fact, a fad which furnishes a certain proof of the purity of the air, that these sudden changes seldom, if ever, passed the health of strangers or Europeans.

In this country agriculture has yet made but small progress. Nova Scotia Is almost a continued for cit, producing every kind of wood which grows in the neiafhbouring provinces of New England. Four fifths of all the lands in the province are covered with pines, ^A■hich are valuable not only soring masts, Ipars, lumber for the sugar plantations, and timber for building, but for yielding tan, pitch, and turpentine, commodities which are all procured from this useful tree, and with which the mother-country may in a few years •t asily be supplied.

All the various species of birch, beech, and maple, and several forts of spruce, are found in all parts in great abundance ; as also numerous herbs and plants, either not common to, or not known in, England. Amongil these none is more plentiful than farfapanlla, and a plant whose root resembles rhubarb in coloui, tate, and effects ; likewise the Indian or mountain tea, and maiden-hair, an herb much in repute for the same purpose, with sin ubi producing strawberries, raspberries, and many other pleasant fruits, with which the woods in summer are well stored : Of these wild produAions the cherries are heft, though . smaller than ours, and growing in bunches somewhat resembling grapes. The sassafras tree grows plentifully in common with otheis ; but amongst them none is more useful to the inhabitants than a species of maple, dilllnguiflied by the name of the sugar tree, as affording a considerable quantity of that valuable ingredient. See Sugar.

Amongst the natural product sons of Nova Scotia, It is necessary to enumerate their iron-ore, which is supposed equally good with that found in any part of A« inerica.

Lime-Hone is likewise found in many places ; It Is extremely good, and is now much used for building : independent of which, it gives the farmers and landholders a great advantage for improving the ground, as it is found by experience to be one of the most approved things in the v/orld for that purpose.

Several of the useful and moll common European bruits have been planted in many places ; so that the
